text:
用工具，不能被使用习惯和沉没成本绑住。

我是codex的重度用户，连续3个月，每月给codex付100美元。用的过程确实帮我省了很多事儿，但最近感觉有点变傻了，尤其写文案、处理复杂任务的时候，没有一开始那么聪明了。

要不是看在codex隔三差五一直在送额度的份上，我早就卸载了。

在群里交流，群友提到grok bot，说可以试试这个，或者把这个和codex搭配着用。刚试用了一会儿，聊几点初步的感受。

1 grok bot除了codex原本拥有的一些功能外，最大的区别之一，是多了一台云端电脑，而且这个云端电脑可以直接在手机上接管使用

也就是说，即便自己没有电脑，也可以让grok bot在他的云端电脑上处理一些复杂任务，而且自己可以实时看到它的处理过程

我前阵子旅游的时候为了实现纯手机远程办公，我用的办法是：codex+uu远程+家里的笔记本电脑持续开机

如果用grok bot，等于我压根就不需要家里那台持续开机的笔记本电脑了

这个对于长期在外，没办法带电脑的人来说，非常实用

2 第二个最大的区别，grok不是项目制了，而是助理制度

我们用 workbuddy，codex的时候，都需要新建项目，一个项目为一个文件夹，每个文件夹里有各种技能skills和规则

但在用grok的时候，没有新建项目，只有新建助理

一个助理可以做一件事儿，也可以做多件事儿，只需要给他安排具体做啥事儿，他就会去做了，而且在手机上就可以操作

看到这个功能，有点感叹，这才是真正懂大多数人工作习惯的Ai，codex在使用体验上，还是有点偏开发性质，要面对一个个文件夹，skill，把简单的事情复杂化

grokbot直接把这些都省略了，对新手来说，更容易理解，更傻瓜式

3 个人感觉，codex道德感比较高，很多事儿不愿意做，比如抓数据，比如做个什么破解软件，就连访问公众号后台，都提示做不了

但grokbot就没这么多洁癖，啥脏活累活都可以直接干，一些codex明确无法访问的网站，交给grokbot后，二话不说给你把数据抓了下来

聊到这里，我突然想到一个搭配：

grokbot既然自带云端电脑，那就直接让它去他的云端电脑上放心大胆地干一些脏活累活，然后在本地电脑上处理一些比较重要，涉及到本地数据的任务

（grok bot自带云端电脑，但他也可以同时操作自己的电脑，等于一个Ai跨电脑操作）

比如我前几天让codex操作我电脑，帮我往红薯和抖音上各怼了50条笔记，为了安全起见，我让它直接操作系统级鼠标指针，完全模拟手动去发，速度也控制地比较慢

那之后可不可以这样，类似的模拟人工操作电脑的繁琐的动作，直接让 grok bot操作云端电脑去干，还有一些数据抓取，刷推荐流找选题，整理选题等动作，也直接让grokbot在云端电脑去做

我自己的电脑腾出来继续做其他更重要的事儿

4 群友聊到一个问题：grokbot作图的能力怎么样？

我发了同一句话给 grokbot 和 codex，下面是他们给我的回复，个人觉得，半斤八两，不会犯大错，对中文的处理也还行，起码比豆包强太多了

做视频还没测试，后面换个号试用的时候再试试

提示词：做一张山西的宣传海报 ，要有山西至少30个景点的预览图 和小字介绍

配图2是grokbot出的，配图3是codex出的。

感觉，相比来说，半斤八两吧，做个图文笔记肯定是足够了，再提示词上再下点功夫，肯定可以和codex媲美了

目前刚试用下来，在日常工作上，grokbot是足够了，做视频和写代码，开发维护小程序怎么样，还不知道，后面换个号再试用一下

如果没啥大问题的话，我就要和codex拜拜了

Ai时代，还是要做个善变的渣男，哪个工具用起来更顺手，就把钱花在哪个上面，不能因为使用习惯和沉没成本，就一直依赖一个落后的工具，干吧！

text:
I asked my Grok Bot Chief of Staff how to improve its memory.

It told me it was already remembering too much.

It’s holding about 1,190 notes. Some are stale. Others contradict each other. That means Grok Bot can answer me from an old version of my business without either of us realising it.

That changed what I’d trust to memory. If I’ve made a standing decision or ruled something out, I want the exact wording in one file or Page my bots can check.

Here’s the prompt I’m using to clean up memory across my Grok Bot team:

"Set up a memory improvement process for me.

1 - Work through my existing notes topic by topic. Find notes that are stale, duplicated or contradict each other. Give me a short list of proposed deletes and merges per topic. Change nothing until I say yes.

2 - Identify notes where the exact wording matters, such as standing decisions, rules and veto lists. Recommend which should become a file or Page instead of a note, and why.

3 - From now on, save rules, not stories. When I make a decision or give a standing instruction, save it as one clear sentence with the date. If it replaces an older note, delete the old one in the same step.

4 - When I say "remember this", save it straight away and confirm in one line.

5 - Keep a Decisions log Page. Each week, add what I decided, with the date, the topic and a link to where it happened.

6 - Every Monday, run a tidy-up and send me proposed deletes and merges. Same rule: change nothing until I say yes.

7 - Before answering anything about the past, check the notes and the Decisions log first, then the chat history. Tell me if you're unsure rather than guessing."

Ask your Bot how many notes it's holding. The number is usually the first surprise.

text:
As all of these outages are getting weird, here is a Grok Bot analysis: 

Verdict: probably not a cyberattack. I'm 8 out of 10 confident. Each outage has its own separate cause, and nobody credible has claimed the FAA one. The FAA hasn't officially closed its root cause yet, so Hawley is right that the full answer isn't public.

Why I don't think it's an attack:

Nothing ties the outages together. They involve different companies, different networks and different failures, with no shared vendor or way https://t.co/HwG0QPgIPR (Nov 12): a bug in code shipped back in July finally got triggered (BleepingComputer, Nov 2026).
Chase (Nov 16): a software update Chase pushed that morning, and an FBI official confirmed that (The Hill, Nov 16).
NSA (Nov 17): it also had an outage today, which it blamed on planned maintenance (Politico, Nov 17).

The FAA failure started the moment a contractor turned on a new router. An L3Harris crew powered up the router in El Dorado, Arkansas during a copper-to-fiber upgrade, and the flood began. The router maker (HPE, which owns Juniper) says the router did exactly what the installer set it up to do (SDxCentral, Nov 17). The FAA then switched off one setting on all 69 new routers, and the problem stopped. That points to a bad setup, not a hacker still inside.
The flood was small. It was about 200–250 connection attempts a second. That's nothing compared with a real flood attack, but plenty to choke 20-year-old equipment. Two newly installed boxes echoing traffic back and forth is a textbook network mistake.
The hacker claims fall apart.A Telegram group, Dark Storm Team, claimed the Outlook outage. Its "proof" was a check it ran almost 5 hours after the outage started (DarknetSearch, Nov 13).
An extortion gang called n0n has JPMorgan listed on its dark web leak site. Chase was on that list since Nov 9, a week before the outage, and the gang claims stolen marketing email records, not that it took systems down (Ransomnews, Nov 16–17).
Nobody anywhere has claimed the FAA outage.

Weeks like this have happened before with no attack. In Oct–Nov 2025, AWS, Azure and Cloudflare each had a global outage within a month, and all three were their own bugs (Cloudflare's report).
Where Hawley has a point:
The FAA knows which device failed, not why. 13 Senate Commerce Democrats said the same thing in a letter and asked for a briefing by Nov 23 (Senate Commerce letter, Nov 16–17).
Accounts of the router conflict. CNN reported the FBI took it. The FBI says it didn't take any equipment (Washington Examiner, Nov 17). Duffy says it's at L3Harris's lab in Florida.
United hasn't given any cause for its Nov 16 outage (AP).
The officials' messaging has been messy. DHS Secretary Mullin said he's 98% sure it's not an attack. On Fox he also floated a rogue "super intelligence" theory from one unnamed contact, and there's no evidence behind it (Fortune, Nov 17).
Risks to this verdict: the lab test of the router in Florida isn't public yet. If it turns up a login nobody can explain, or software that doesn't match the factory version, the picture changes. Separately, a real attack did hit about 178 websites through a third-party tool on Nov 16, but it didn't take anything offline (Malwarebytes).
What I checked on X and the dark web: on X, the network engineers mostly blame a misconfigured router, and I found no believable insider saying it was an attack. For the dark web, the trackers that watch ransomware leak sites show nothing new against the FAA or L3Harris this week.
What to watch: the L3Harris lab findings, the FAA's Senate briefing due by Nov 23, Microsoft's final report, and whether n0n actually posts the JPMorgan data around Nov 18. I can recheck after the Nov 23 briefing if you want.

A reminder that never arrives is worse than no reminder at all.

Last week one of my Grok Bot reminders didn't show up. It was a nudge to extend my parking before it ran out. The run started, failed, and nothing reached me.

What I liked was what happened next. It didn't just resend it and move on. It looked for the weak spot and found it: that reminder lived in one place, with no saved copy, no retry and no backup.

So it fixed the setup. Parking reminders now also land on my calendar with a popup 30 minutes before the end time. Chat reminders keep a pending/delivered record and try once more if the first attempt doesn't land.

That's the part of running bots nobody talks about. Things break. The useful question is whether the fix makes the next miss less likely.

If you run automations, how do you catch the ones that fail silently?

text:
My AI agent clocks in at 8 AM. I don't. ☕

Every morning it reads the top 10 Hacker News stories, summarizes them, and leaves the brief waiting for me.

It's Hermes, an open-source agent, running on a phone in the @Acurast network.

The setup:
→ Acurast's Cargo runtime runs full Linux containers, so a Python agent just works
→ Hermes brings the scheduler, memory and a web UI
→ OpenRouter plugs in whatever model you like
→ acurast deploy, confirm the fee, get a URL
→ type the task once in plain English

No VPS. No babysitting a server. Close the laptop, it keeps working.

One thing to know: it runs for as long as your deployment runs. When it ends, the phone is released and the data is wiped. Pick the duration with that in mind.

Most AI demos answer one question.
The useful ones do the same job every day without being asked.

That job has to run somewhere. Mine runs on someone's phone.

2. When a task gets stuck waiting on me, the bot asks once and goes quiet. I had to say "you forgot me". Give it a nudge after a few hours.

3. No usage meter per bot. I hit my limits and had to pause everything blind, without knowing which bot was burning it.

4. Bots can't share one goal. Let me give 3 bots one target ("5 interviews in November") and see one progress board.

Fix these and it's a real chief of staff.
